sections.title: BACKGROUND

summary.text: Explains the background to the 2019 update: the 2018 interim guidance preferring dolutegravir (DTG) regimens, caution over a neural tube defect signal in Botswana, and gaps in evidence on efavirenz 400 mg. It then sets out the updated recommendations in a box, naming DTG-based regimens as preferred first- and second-line therapy, efavirenz 400 mg and raltegravir as alternatives, with strength and certainty ratings.

sections.extract: In 2018, WHO published interim guidelines recommending dolutegravir (DTG)-containing regimens as the preferred first- and second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens for people living with HIV (1). sections.title: DTG IN FIRST-LINE ART

summary.text: Summarizes the 2019 systematic review showing DTG-based first-line therapy outperforms efavirenz on viral suppression, discontinuation and resistance, with fewer drug interactions and activity against HIV-2. It notes risks of sleep problems and weight gain and says women should receive information on benefits and risks of DTG at conception to make informed choices.

sections.extract: An updated systematic review conducted in 2019 to support the guidelines reaffirmed that a first-line regimen of DTG combined with two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) leads to higher viral suppression and lower risk of discontinuing treatment and developing HIV drug resistance compared with EFV-based regimens among treatment- naive adults. sections.title: to women exposed to DTG before conception or early in pregnancy

summary.text: Updates the evidence on neural tube defects among infants born to women taking DTG at conception, reporting a fall in the Tsepamo study estimate to 0.30% and additional surveillance data from Botswana. It places the absolute risk as very low, notes the role of folate fortification and calls for continued surveillance, and concludes that modelling favours DTG on balance and cost-effectiveness.

sections.extract: Although the prevalence of neural tube defects associated with using DTG at conception in the Tsepamo study has declined from 0.94% (4 of 426 exposures) to 0.30% (5 of 1683 exposures), the prevalence difference remains statistically significantly higher than all other ARV drug exposure groups. sections.title: Box 3: A woman-centred approach

summary.text: Describes a woman-centred, human rights-based approach to antiretroviral therapy that respects women's autonomy and informed choice. It then covers DTG approval and formulations for children, raltegravir as an option from birth, and the need for twice-daily DTG in people with HIV and TB on rifampicin.

sections.extract: Woman-centred health services involve an approach to health care that consciously adopts the perspectives of women and their families and communities. This means that health services see women as active participants in and beneficiaries of trusted health systems that respond to women’s needs, rights and preferences in humane and holistic ways (with no coercion). sections.title: EFV 400 mg in first-line ART

summary.text: Reviews evidence showing efavirenz 400 mg is better tolerated than the 600 mg dose, with similar viral suppression, lower cost and expected safety in pregnancy. It discusses limited data on its use with rifampicin-based TB treatment and its pharmacokinetics in pregnancy. It then introduces the review of DTG for people whose non-DTG first-line regimen has failed, finding DTG generally outperforms protease-inhibitor-based second-line therapy on safety and efficacy.

sections.extract: The updated systematic review found that EFV 400 mg is better tolerated than EFV in standard dose (EFV 600 mg), with lower risk of treatment discontinuation and severe treatment- related adverse events. Regimens containing EFV 400 mg and EFV 600 mg were comparable for viral suppression, mortality and mental and nervous system adverse events. sections.title: DTG in second-line ART

summary.text: Recommends DTG as the preferred second-line drug for adults, adolescents and children failing non-DTG first-line regimens, and a boosted protease inhibitor for those failing DTG-based first-line therapy. Table 2 lists preferred and alternative second-line regimens by population and failing regimen, with footnotes on dosing and use in children.

sections.extract: Taken together with other advantages, including lower cost, less potential for drug–drug interactions, lower pill burden and availability in once-daily fixed-dose combinations, DTG is recommended as the preferred ARV drug for second-line ART among adults, adolescents and children for whom a non-DTG-based first-line regimen has failed. summary.text: A section heading fragment on transitioning national HIV programmes to DTG and efavirenz 400 mg.

sections.title: Clinical and implementation considerations

summary.text: Describes manufacturing capacity for DTG and progress by countries in adopting efavirenz 400 mg and DTG into guidelines and procurement. It sets out drug–drug interaction cautions, such as with certain anticonvulsants and cation-containing antacids and supplements, and advises a phased transition with buffer stocks. Tables summarize considerations for transitioning adults, adolescents and children who are stable on ART to optimal regimens.

sections.extract: considerations Multiple suppliers are capable of manufacturing DTG as a single product and as part of a fixed-dose combination and have already begun expanding capacity to cope with the increased demand. No shortfalls in manufacturing capacity are currently anticipated, although countries should undertake effective supply planning.
